name: English Medieval Timber Frame

revival_periods.note: Half-timbering returns as applied decoration over a stud or masonry wall. Almost all Victorian and later 'black-and-white' work is non-structural, and the applied version arrives in America as Tudor Revival.

geography.hearth: The wooded lowland belt — Kent and Sussex Weald, East Anglia, the West Midlands, Cheshire and the Welsh Marches

lineage.note: The carpenters who framed a manorial hall roof and those who framed a cathedral roof were the same trade working from the same geometry. Moulded arch-braces, cusped wind-braces and crown-post capitals in houses are Gothic details executed by carpenters rather than borrowed from masons.

description.short: The native carpentry tradition of lowland Britain, in which a jointed frame of oak carries the whole building and the wall between the timbers is merely infill.
description.long:
This is the tradition that never came from anywhere. Masonry arrived with the Normans; timber framing was already here, continuous from Anglo-Saxon practice, and it simply kept going, absorbing Gothic taste at the level of moulding while never changing its structural logic. Two systems coexist. The cruck frame pairs curved blades rising from ground to ridge, each pair cut from a single tree split in half so the two blades are mirror images — a building conceived as a sequence of arches, dominant in the west and north. The box frame builds a rectilinear cage of sill, post, tie-beam and plate, braced diagonally, and is the ancestor of every later Anglo-American frame. Above both sits the carpented roof: crown-post and collar-purlin in the south-east, arch-braced collar trusses in the west, hammerbeams where money and ambition met.

What produced it was oak, and a very particular economy of oak. England had enough timber and not enough cash; a frame could be cut, jointed and numbered in a framing yard, then reared by a village in a day, whereas masonry needed quarries, carts, lime and a season of curing. Because the frame carries everything, the wall panels can be wattle and daub, brick nogging or lath and plaster without altering the structure, which is why the same house may show three different infills from three different centuries. The jetty — an upper floor cantilevered forward on projecting joists — is the tradition's most-argued detail; the honest structural account is that it lets the upper floor joists be shorter and stiffer while gaining floor area, and the honest social account is that it was also showing off, since a jetty costs timber and announces it.

The fifteenth-century Wealden house is the type's masterpiece and the clearest case of a plan producing a form. An open hall in the centre, two-storeyed bays at each end jettied forward, and one great hipped roof carried across all three on a deep sprocketed eave: from outside, a recessed centre under a continuous overhang, which reads as a single deliberate composition and is in fact a direct expression of the hall-and-crosswing plan. When wall fireplaces and chimney stacks became affordable in the sixteenth century — the 'Great Rebuilding' Hoskins identified between roughly 1570 and 1640 — the open hall was floored over, a stack was inserted in the screens passage, and thousands of these houses acquired the chambers upstairs that they still have.

Standing inside one is unlike any masonry interior. The room is defined by lines rather than surfaces: posts, braces and joists divide the space into a visible cage, and because oak moves as it dries, none of those lines is quite straight. Ceilings are low, sills are high, and the floor gives slightly. There is a strong sense of the building as an assembly of pieces that could in principle be taken apart — which is literally true, and many have been, dismantled and re-erected elsewhere with their carpenters' assembly marks still legible on the joints. That legibility is the tradition's deepest gift to a kit-of-parts system: every joint in a medieval frame was numbered before it was ever raised.

defining_characteristics: A jointed hardwood frame — cruck or box — carrying all vertical and lateral load, with wall panels as non-structural infill
Mortice-and-tenon joints secured by riven oak pegs; no metal fasteners in the primary frame
Structural bays of 3.0-5.0 m set by the length of available oak and expressed on the elevation as panel divisions
A carpented roof designed to be seen — crown-post, arch-braced collar or hammerbeam — over the open hall
Infill panels of wattle and daub, later brick nogging or plaster, sitting flush or slightly recessed behind the timber face
Jettied upper floors on projecting joists, with the jetty bressumer moulded and the joist ends exposed or boarded
Steep roof pitch (48-55 degrees) demanded by thatch, stone slate or plain clay tile
diagnostic_tells: Timbers of irregular section and slight curvature, wide panels in the south-east and small close studding in East Anglia — the closer the studs, the wealthier the builder, since close studding is a deliberate waste of oak
Carpenters' assembly marks (chiselled Roman numerals) at the joints, and empty peg holes where members have been reused from an earlier frame
A jetty that returns around a corner with a dragon beam set diagonally at 45 degrees — a detail that cannot be faked convincingly and is absent from all applied half-timbering
Wall panels that are not rectangles: curved braces cutting across the panel field, and quatrefoil or herringbone patterned panels in Cheshire and the Welsh Marches
A massive brick or stone stack inserted awkwardly into a frame it clearly post-dates, usually in the old screens passage — the signature of the Great Rebuilding

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor is a period and a taste that timber framing passed through, not an alternative to it. Tudor at the great-house scale is brick and stone with four-centred arches and symmetrical gatehouse fronts; timber framing is the underlying carpentry tradition of the same decades at every scale below that.

The cottage tradition is the same carpentry at the bottom of the social scale, and in the west it is often not carpentry at all but cob or rubble. Timber frame proper is a merchant's and yeoman's architecture with a designed frame; the cottage is what is left when the frame budget is a quarter of that.

Parallel rather than derived. Continental Fachwerk uses much closer studding with carved and painted sill beams, wall panels usually smaller and more decorated, and roofs framed with principal rafters and purlins rather than the English crown-post. English work leaves the oak to silver; the black-and-white paint scheme is largely a Victorian addition.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The structural bay of the frame. Everything — panel width, window width, jetty depth, roof truss spacing — is a division of a bay, and the bay is set by the length of sound oak a carpenter could get, roughly 4.5 m at the limit. There is no applied proportional theory of any kind.
typical_ratios: Bay length 3.0-5.0 m; hall of two bays, crosswings of one to two
Wall panel roughly square in the south-east (1.0-1.4 m), and 1:3 to 1:4 vertical in East Anglian close studding
Post section 200-300 mm square; tie beam 250-350 mm deep
Jetty projection 350-600 mm, roughly one third of the floor joist depth times four — never the exaggerated overhang of revival work
Roof pitch 48-55 degrees; eave height 2.1-2.7 m at the wall plate
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Visible and insistent: principal posts every 3.0-5.0 m carry the tie beams and truss, with secondary studs subdividing. Openings are cut within the panel field and never cross a principal post, so window widths are dictated by the frame rather than the other way round.

massing_affinities.note: The hall with jettied crosswings at both ends — the Wealden and half-H types are the tradition's central form.
The single-bay open hall, the irreducible unit before crosswings are added.
The post-Rebuilding condition, hall and parlour either side of an inserted lobby-entry stack.
Jettied timber street ranges in Lavenham, Shrewsbury, Chester and York, party-walled and gable-end or eaves-on to the street.
The jetty is precisely the ancestor of the American garrison overhang, which survived across the Atlantic as a decorative memory after the structural reason had gone.

constraints.statement: Timber positions must be structurally derivable: every vertical member reaches a sill or a beam, every brace resolves a corner, and no timber terminates in mid-panel. Applied patterning that does not correspond to a frame is forbidden.
Jetty projection 350-600 mm. Below 300 mm the shadow line fails to register; above 750 mm the building reads as twentieth-century Tudor Revival caricature.

test.note: 300mm and 750mm are the statement's illustrative failure points, not additional bounds -- the stated range is 350-600mm.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees, and not less than 50 degrees under thatch. Infill panels must be set behind the timber face so that water is thrown clear of the joint, never proud of it.

test.note: Tests the universal floor (45deg). Thatch's stricter 50deg floor is material-conditional and stays prose, as does the infill-panel weathering clause.

constraints.statement: Openings are cut within a panel and may not interrupt a principal post or tie beam; window width is therefore a whole number of stud bays.
Where a masonry stack occurs in a frame of pre-1550 character it should read as an insertion — full-height, of different material, breaking the panel grid — because that is what it historically is.

exemplars.name: Alfriston Clergy House
exemplars.note: A fourteenth-century Wealden hall house, thatched, with its open hall and chalk-and-sour-milk floor intact; the first building bought by the National Trust, in 1896.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1191431 describes a 'C14 timber-framed and close-studded building of wealden type' whose interior 'retains its open hall with crown-post exposed', and quotes the tablet recording that the National Trust bought and repaired it in 1898; both statements are the register's.

exemplars.name: Paycocke's House
exemplars.note: A cloth merchant's house with elaborate close studding, a richly carved jetty bressumer and moulded ceiling beams — timber framing used as conspicuous display of wool wealth.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1337597 gives the frame bay by bay -- a five-bay main range of c.1505 cut down from three storeys to two about 1600, with the sawn-off rear posts still readable inside -- which is the kind of statement a kit figure can be held against; the judgment is this project's.

exemplars.name: Little Moreton Hall
exemplars.note: North range 1504-08, west range 1546, south range with the Long Gallery c.1560-62. The West Midlands patterned-panel tradition at its most extravagant and least structurally disciplined; the gallery is visibly deforming the frame beneath it.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1161988 says the present appearance 'is the result of at least seven builds' and records the strengthening collar-beams and iron tie-rods added under the Long Gallery; that it is the building the West Midlands patterned tradition is known by is this project's judgment, resting on the register's account of the fabric.

exemplars.name: Lavenham Guildhall of Corpus Christi
exemplars.note: East Anglian close studding at full strength, in a town where the wool trade collapsed early enough that nobody could afford to rebuild in brick.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1037186 calls it 'one of the finest examples of half timbering in this part of the country', which is a regional claim in the register's own words; the standing follows those words rather than the stronger note on this exemplar.

exemplars.name: Speke Hall
exemplars.note: Historic England 1359837: 'South range of 1490-1506, east and west ranges of c.1540-1560, North range of 1598. For Norris Family. Timber frame on stone base with stone lateral stacks. Stone slate roof. 2 storeys with attic, courtyard plan.' The year here is the earlier end of the south range's dates as the entry prints them; the Wikipedia infobox instead gives 1530-1598.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1359837 calls it 'One of the most important timber framed manor houses in the country'; that judgment is the register's.

exemplars.name: Leigh Court Barn
exemplars.note: Historic England 1349245: a cruck-framed barn of ten bays, 'Probably C14', which radiocarbon dating 'although not conclusive, suggests' is C14 'with a date of c1325 likely'. 140 feet long, trusses nearly 33 feet high spanning 34 feet -- 'the largest cruck building in the country'. It is a barn and not a house, and it is here because the cruck frame is half of what this node claims as its structure and no dwelling among its exemplars is cruck-framed.
exemplars.why: Historic England 1349245 calls it 'the largest cruck building in the country' and states three linear dimensions -- 140 ft long, trusses nearly 33 ft high spanning 34 ft -- which is exactly why it is here to be measured; the superlative and the figures are both the register's.

sources: R. W. Brunskill, Timber Building in Britain (1985)
R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)
W. G. Hoskins, 'The Rebuilding of Rural England 1570-1640', Past and Present 4 (1953)
Margaret Wood, The English Mediaeval House (1965)

proportion_packs.note: The node that states this pack's central rule for it, in one sentence holding both families: 'wall panel roughly square in the south-east (1.0-1.4 m), and 1:3 to 1:4 vertical in East Anglian close studding'. Primary, and it also supplies the post section at 200-300 mm, the tie beam at 250-350, the jetty at 350-600, and the sentence the whole pack rests on -- the frame carries 'all vertical and lateral load, with wall panels as non-structural infill'. `timber-bay` stays bound and is not displaced: it owns the frame -- bay, storey, depth, pitch -- and this pack owns what fills it, and neither restates the other.

english-medieval-timber-frame is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to, and it is effectively the pack's anchor node: the pack's own authority note is 'reconstructed by measurement from surviving English and Anglo-American box frames,' and this style's proportional_system states the bay IS the governing logic ('Everything — panel width, window width, jetty depth, roof truss spacing — is a division of a bay... There is no applied proportional theory of any kind'). The pack's jetty, depth-and-pile and window-grouping rules map directly onto this style's own defining characteristics.

The ancestor, and the node the pack's structural reasoning comes from -- this is the jetty that carries a whole storey of wall on the joist ends, which is why its multiple is four thirds of the joist depth and not the garrisons' two. Its own record notes the descent: 'the jetty is precisely the ancestor of the American garrison overhang, which survived across the Atlantic as a decorative memory after the structural reason had gone.' It also supplies the dragon beam, the one detail in the pack that `english-medieval-timber-frame` says cannot be faked. Behind `timber-panel` and `timber-bay`, which own the frame and its infill; this owns only what happens where a floor leaves the wall.

The node that says WHY the bay is what it is: 'the bay is set by the length of sound oak a carpenter could get, roughly 4.5 m at the limit', and 'there is no applied proportional theory of any kind'. Its statement of the pack's central claim is the most operational of the four -- 'openings are cut within the panel field and never cross a principal post, so window widths are dictated by the frame rather than the other way round'. Behind `timber-panel`, `timber-bay` and `jetty-overhang`, which own the frame, its infill and its overhang; this owns only what the frame does to the elevation.

english-medieval-timber-frame is named directly in room-vernacular's applies_to. The two packs are complementary by design (room-vernacular's own module note explicitly distinguishes the room from the bay that contains it), and this style's hall-and-parlor and hall-single-cell massing affinities are literally room-vernacular's own worked examples.

Bound for the opening in a timber wall rather than a stone one, which changes the material and not the geometry: the mullion is oak, the light is the same width, the leaded panel is the same, and the label is a moulded timber head. `timber-panel` holds this node's wall and this pack its openings, and the two meet at a real constraint the pack should be read with -- a framed wall is 150 mm thick against a rubble wall's 500-700, so there is no deep reveal here and no window seat, and the openings sit almost flush. Everything the pack says about drainage and the reveal applies with less depth to work with.
